title: Learn Cryptography in Go
description: Practice cryptographic concepts in Go, from encodings and classical ciphers to authenticated encryption, signatures, and password-storage policy.

lessons.title: Cryptography Is More Than Encryption
lessons.instruction: Cryptography can protect confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. Encryption addresses confidentiality; other primitives answer whether data changed and who produced it. Complete the list of core properties.

lessons.title: What Is Cryptography?
lessons.instruction: Choose primitives by the property required. Encryption hides plaintext, while a keyed MAC detects changes and authenticates a party that knows the shared key. Correct the property assigned to HMAC.

lessons.title: Shared-Key Encryption
lessons.instruction: Symmetric encryption requires both parties to possess the same secret key. Make the sender and receiver use the same key; never transmit that secret alongside the ciphertext.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	senderKey := "blue-key"
	receiverKey := "red-key"
	fmt.Println(senderKey == receiverKey)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	senderKey := "blue-key"
	receiverKey := "blue-key"
	fmt.Println(senderKey == receiverKey)
}

lessons.title: Hybrid Encryption
lessons.instruction: Public-key operations are useful for establishing a secret, while fast symmetric encryption protects the payload. Assign each job to the appropriate key type.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	wrapSessionKeyWith := "session-key"
	encryptPayloadWith := "public-key"
	fmt.Println(wrapSessionKeyWith, encryptPayloadWith)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	wrapSessionKeyWith := "public-key"
	encryptPayloadWith := "session-key"
	fmt.Println(wrapSessionKeyWith, encryptPayloadWith)
}

lessons.title: Better Keys
lessons.instruction: Encryption keys need unpredictable bytes from crypto/rand, not timestamps, math/rand, or memorable text. Allocate a 32-byte key and let crypto/rand fill it.

lessons.title: Cryptology, Cryptography, and Cryptanalysis
lessons.instruction: Cryptology covers both building protection and studying how to defeat it. Label secure-system design as cryptography and attack analysis as cryptanalysis.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	design := "cryptology"
	attackStudy := "cryptology"
	fmt.Println(design, attackStudy)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	design := "cryptography"
	attackStudy := "cryptanalysis"
	fmt.Println(design, attackStudy)
}

lessons.title: Single-Use Keys
lessons.instruction: A one-time pad XORs plaintext with a uniformly random key of equal length. Its key must remain secret and must never be reused. Apply the two-byte teaching pad; this is a demonstration, not a production cipher.

lessons.title: Single-Use Keys Review
lessons.instruction: Reusing an XOR pad cancels the key when two ciphertexts are XORed, exposing the XOR of their plaintexts. Reuse one key below to demonstrate that failure.

lessons.title: Encoding Bytes
lessons.instruction: Hex encoding represents each byte with two printable characters. Encode the UTF-8 bytes for Go; the result is portable text, not secret data.

lessons.title: Encoding Is Not Encryption
lessons.instruction: Base64 has no key and anyone can reverse it. Decode the public representation R28= to show why encoding cannot provide confidentiality.

lessons.title: Formatting
lessons.instruction: Base64 URL encoding replaces characters that conflict with URLs. Use raw URL-safe base64 for the two bytes so the result has neither +, /, nor padding.

lessons.title: Decoding
lessons.instruction: Decoders reject malformed input, so applications must check the returned error before using bytes. Supply valid base64 for Go and report successful decoding.

lessons.title: Alphabet Formula
lessons.instruction: A fixed-length key made from A possible symbols has A^L candidates. Set the length so a 26-character alphabet produces 17,576 three-character keys.

lessons.title: Brute-Force Attacks
lessons.instruction: Attack cost depends on both the keyspace and the guess rate. Divide one million candidates by one thousand guesses per second to estimate the worst-case seconds.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	keyspace := 100_000
	guessesPerSecond := 1_000
	fmt.Println(keyspace / guessesPerSecond)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	keyspace := 1_000_000
	guessesPerSecond := 1_000
	fmt.Println(keyspace / guessesPerSecond)
}

lessons.title: Crack an Insecure Key
lessons.instruction: Tiny secrets can be exhausted quickly. Search every two-digit PIN and print the matching candidate; this toy search is why real keys need large, random keyspaces.

lessons.title: Entropy
lessons.instruction: Uniformly choosing one of 256 byte values contributes eight bits of entropy. Set the length to four independent bytes and calculate the total entropy.

lessons.title: What Is a Cipher?
lessons.instruction: A cipher is a keyed, reversible transformation between plaintext and ciphertext. A hash is deliberately one-way, so it is not a cipher. Correct the description.

lessons.title: Caesar Cipher
lessons.instruction: The Caesar cipher rotates letters through a 26-character alphabet. Implement the shift with wraparound to turn HELLO into KHOOR. This historical cipher is not secure.

lessons.title: Caesar Cipher Security
lessons.instruction: A Caesar ciphertext has only 26 possible shifts, including the identity shift. Set the attack to enumerate the complete keyspace; modern ciphers rely on vastly larger keys.

lessons.title: Exclusive Or (XOR)
lessons.instruction: XOR sets a bit when its two input bits differ. Replace OR with XOR so binary 110 combined with 011 produces binary 101.

lessons.title: XOR Reversibility
lessons.instruction: Applying the same XOR key twice restores the original value: (message XOR key) XOR key equals message. Use the same key for both operations.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	message, key := byte(0x5a), byte(0xc3)
	ciphertext := message ^ key
	recovered := ciphertext ^ 0x11
	fmt.Println(recovered == message)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	message, key := byte(0x5a), byte(0xc3)
	ciphertext := message ^ key
	recovered := ciphertext ^ key
	fmt.Println(recovered == message)
}

lessons.title: One-Time Pad
lessons.instruction: A one-time pad decrypts only when the receiver has the exact random pad used once by the sender. Recover the message with the original pad. This tiny fixture demonstrates the rule; it is not key management.

lessons.title: Perfect Security
lessons.instruction: Perfect secrecy for a one-time pad requires a uniformly random secret key as long as the message and no key reuse. Correct the reuse condition.

lessons.title: Keystreams
lessons.instruction: A stream cipher combines plaintext with a pseudorandom keystream, commonly through XOR. Apply the teaching keystream to GO. Real systems use authenticated constructions, not this fixed example.

lessons.title: Streaming Encryption
lessons.instruction: Go's cipher.Stream can transform arbitrary-length data. Use the identical key and initial counter for decryption. CTR alone does not authenticate data; production designs should use an AEAD.
lessons.starter:
package main

import (
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key := make([]byte, 16)
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(key)
	iv := make([]byte, aes.BlockSize)
	message := []byte("stream data")
	ciphertext := make([]byte, len(message))
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(ciphertext, message)
	wrongIV := append([]byte(nil), iv...)
	wrongIV[len(wrongIV)-1] = 1
	recovered := make([]byte, len(message))
	cipher.NewCTR(block, wrongIV).XORKeyStream(recovered, ciphertext)
	fmt.Println(string(recovered) == string(message))
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key := make([]byte, 16)
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(key)
	iv := make([]byte, aes.BlockSize)
	message := []byte("stream data")
	ciphertext := make([]byte, len(message))
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(ciphertext, message)
	recovered := make([]byte, len(message))
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(recovered, ciphertext)
	fmt.Println(string(recovered) == string(message))
}

lessons.title: Cipher State
lessons.instruction: A stream object advances its keystream position after every byte. Encrypt two chunks with one continuous stream so their result matches one-shot processing. CTR remains an unauthenticated teaching example here.
lessons.starter:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(make([]byte, 16))
	iv := make([]byte, aes.BlockSize)
	oneShot := make([]byte, 10)
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(oneShot, []byte("helloworld"))
	chunked := make([]byte, 10)
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(chunked[:5], []byte("hello"))
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(chunked[5:], []byte("world"))
	fmt.Println(bytes.Equal(oneShot, chunked))
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(make([]byte, 16))
	iv := make([]byte, aes.BlockSize)
	oneShot := make([]byte, 10)
	cipher.NewCTR(block, iv).XORKeyStream(oneShot, []byte("helloworld"))
	chunked := make([]byte, 10)
	stream := cipher.NewCTR(block, iv)
	stream.XORKeyStream(chunked[:5], []byte("hello"))
	stream.XORKeyStream(chunked[5:], []byte("world"))
	fmt.Println(bytes.Equal(oneShot, chunked))
}

lessons.title: State Reuse
lessons.instruction: Reusing a CTR key and initial counter repeats the keystream, so XORing ciphertexts exposes the XOR of plaintexts. Reuse the IV only to demonstrate this failure; never do it in a real system.

lessons.title: Block Ciphers
lessons.instruction: A block cipher transforms one fixed-size block under a key. AES uses 16-byte blocks. Set the payload to two complete blocks; applications still need a secure mode such as GCM.

lessons.title: Block vs. Stream
lessons.instruction: A stream interface accepts arbitrary lengths, while a raw block operation requires exact block alignment. Check the 24-byte message against AES's real block size.

lessons.title: Block Sizes
lessons.instruction: AES always has a 16-byte block size, independent of whether its key is 16, 24, or 32 bytes. Print the package constant rather than guessing from the key.

lessons.title: Chunks Review
lessons.instruction: Raw block processing advances exactly one block at a time. Count the AES-sized chunks in a 32-byte buffer. This lesson concerns boundaries, not an encryption mode.

lessons.title: Key Schedules
lessons.instruction: A key schedule derives round keys from the original key. Complete three rounds of this tiny rotation model to see the progression. It is intentionally not AES and must never protect data.

lessons.title: Key Schedule Review
lessons.instruction: AES expands 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys for 10, 12, and 14 rounds respectively. Complete the lookup for the 32-byte key.

lessons.title: Feistel Rounds
lessons.instruction: A Feistel round sends the old right half left and XORs the old left with a round function. Complete one small round to understand the structure; this toy function is not secure encryption.

lessons.title: Feistel Decryption
lessons.instruction: A Feistel round is reversible even when its round function is not. Recover the original halves from the prior round by applying the inverse relationship.

lessons.title: Data Encryption Standard
lessons.instruction: DES has an 8-byte block and an effective 56-bit key. NIST withdrew it because that keyspace is no longer secure. Inspect its block size while keeping its status explicit: historical only.

lessons.title: DES Review
lessons.instruction: Although a DES key is stored in eight bytes, parity bits leave only 56 effective key bits. Record that strength and reject DES as a modern choice.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	effectiveBits := 64
	useForNewSystems := true
	fmt.Println(effectiveBits, useForNewSystems)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	effectiveBits := 56
	useForNewSystems := false
	fmt.Println(effectiveBits, useForNewSystems)
}

lessons.title: Initialization Vectors
lessons.instruction: CBC requires a fresh, unpredictable IV exactly one block long. Generate an 8-byte DES-sized IV only to inspect the historical mode's requirement; use modern authenticated encryption for real data.

lessons.title: DES Feistel Network
lessons.instruction: DES applies multiple keyed Feistel rounds; decryption uses the round keys in reverse order. Make the toy encrypt and decrypt paths use the same two rounds. This model is instructional, not DES security.

lessons.title: S-Box Lookup
lessons.instruction: An S-box replaces a small input with a table value to introduce nonlinearity. Read row 1, column 2 from this reduced teaching table; it is not a complete DES S-box.

lessons.title: S-Box Row and Column
lessons.instruction: For a DES-style six-bit S-box input, the outer bits select the row and the middle four select the column. Extract both indices from binary 100011.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	input := byte(0b100011)
	row := (input >> 4) & 0b11
	column := input & 0b1111
	fmt.Println(row, column)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	input := byte(0b100011)
	row := ((input & 0b100000) >> 4) | (input & 1)
	column := (input >> 1) & 0b1111
	fmt.Println(row, column)
}

lessons.title: AES Keys and Blocks
lessons.instruction: AES accepts 16-, 24-, or 32-byte keys and always uses 16-byte blocks. Supply a valid 16-byte key and confirm construction succeeds; use random key material outside this exercise.

lessons.title: Authenticated Encryption with AES-GCM
lessons.instruction: AES-GCM encrypts and authenticates both the ciphertext and optional associated data. Open the message with the same associated header used by Seal; never replace an AEAD with raw AES blocks.

lessons.title: Nonces
lessons.instruction: A GCM nonce is not secret, but it must be unique for every message under one key. Allocate the AEAD's required nonce size and fill it from crypto/rand.

lessons.title: Nonce and Tag Review
lessons.instruction: GCM's authentication tag makes modified ciphertext fail closed. Tamper with one byte and confirm Open rejects it. Nonce uniqueness is still mandatory even when the tag is checked.
lessons.starter:
package main

import (
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(make([]byte, 16))
	gcm, _ := cipher.NewGCM(block)
	nonce := make([]byte, gcm.NonceSize())
	ciphertext := gcm.Seal(nil, nonce, []byte("message"), nil)
	_, err := gcm.Open(nil, nonce, ciphertext, nil)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(make([]byte, 16))
	gcm, _ := cipher.NewGCM(block)
	nonce := make([]byte, gcm.NonceSize())
	ciphertext := gcm.Seal(nil, nonce, []byte("message"), nil)
	ciphertext[0] ^= 1
	_, err := gcm.Open(nil, nonce, ciphertext, nil)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}

lessons.title: Asymmetric Encryption
lessons.instruction: Public-key encryption lets a sender encrypt with the recipient's public key and the recipient decrypt with the private key. Correct the direction of those operations.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	encryptWith := "private"
	decryptWith := "public"
	fmt.Printf("encrypt=%s decrypt=%s\n", encryptWith, decryptWith)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	encryptWith := "public"
	decryptWith := "private"
	fmt.Printf("encrypt=%s decrypt=%s\n", encryptWith, decryptWith)
}

lessons.title: Public and Private Keys
lessons.instruction: For signatures, the private key signs and the public key verifies. Sign with one Ed25519 key pair and verify with its matching public key; signing proves authenticity but does not hide the message.

lessons.title: RSA
lessons.instruction: An RSA public key contains the modulus n and public exponent e; the private exponent d must remain secret. Complete the component labels before studying the arithmetic.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	publicParts := "n"
	privatePart := "e"
	fmt.Printf("public=%s private=%s\n", publicParts, privatePart)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	publicParts := "n,e"
	privatePart := "d"
	fmt.Printf("public=%s private=%s\n", publicParts, privatePart)
}

lessons.title: RSA vs. Elliptic-Curve Cryptography
lessons.instruction: RSA and elliptic-curve systems use different mathematics and key representations; byte lengths are not directly comparable security measures. Record a common 2048-bit RSA modulus beside Ed25519's 32-byte public key.

lessons.title: RSA Key Generation
lessons.instruction: Generate RSA keys with crypto/rand and validate them; never choose primes by hand. Use a 2048-bit modulus for this exercise and prefer protocol-specific modern guidance in production.

lessons.title: Totient and E
lessons.instruction: In textbook RSA arithmetic, φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1), and e must be coprime with φ(n). Use e=17 for the classic tiny p=61, q=53 example. These numbers are educational only.

lessons.title: Modular Exponentiation
lessons.instruction: RSA computes powers modulo n without constructing the enormous full power. Finish square-and-multiply for 65^17 mod 3233. This is textbook arithmetic, not padded RSA encryption.

lessons.title: Modular Congruence
lessons.instruction: Two integers are congruent modulo n when they leave the same remainder. Check that 35 and 11 are congruent modulo 12.

lessons.title: RSA-OAEP Encryption
lessons.instruction: Practical RSA encryption requires randomized padding. Encrypt with OAEP and decrypt with the same hash and context label; do not use textbook RSA or PKCS #1 v1.5 encryption for new designs.
lessons.starter:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/rsa"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key, _ := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)
	message := []byte("session key")
	ciphertext, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, message, []byte("course"))
	plaintext, err := rsa.DecryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, key, ciphertext, []byte("wrong"))
	fmt.Println(err == nil && bytes.Equal(plaintext, message))
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/rsa"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key, _ := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)
	message := []byte("session key")
	label := []byte("course")
	ciphertext, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, message, label)
	plaintext, err := rsa.DecryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, key, ciphertext, label)
	fmt.Println(err == nil && bytes.Equal(plaintext, message))
}

lessons.title: Multiplicative Inverse
lessons.instruction: The private exponent d is the multiplicative inverse of e modulo φ(n). Search the full toy range to find the inverse of 17 modulo 3120; real libraries derive this internally.

lessons.title: Private Key
lessons.instruction: The toy exponents must satisfy e·d ≡ 1 mod φ(n). Set d to the derived private exponent and confirm the relationship. Never log or expose a real private exponent or prime factors.

lessons.title: Textbook RSA Decryption
lessons.instruction: For the tiny teaching key, decryption computes c^d mod n. Use d=2753 to recover numeric message 65 from ciphertext 2790. Real applications must use RSA-OAEP instead of this unpadded operation.

lessons.title: RSA-OAEP Round Trip
lessons.instruction: OAEP randomness makes two encryptions of the same message differ, while either can still decrypt with the private key. Confirm both properties with Go's RSA implementation.
lessons.starter:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/rsa"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key, _ := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)
	message := []byte("payload")
	c1, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, message, nil)
	c2, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, message, nil)
	plaintext, err := rsa.DecryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, key, c1, nil)
	different := bytes.Equal(c1, c2)
	fmt.Println(different, err == nil && bytes.Equal(plaintext, message))
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/rsa"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key, _ := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)
	message := []byte("payload")
	c1, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, message, nil)
	c2, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, message, nil)
	plaintext, err := rsa.DecryptOAEP(sha256.New(), rand.Reader, key, c1, nil)
	different := !bytes.Equal(c1, c2)
	fmt.Println(different, err == nil && bytes.Equal(plaintext, message))
}

lessons.title: Hash Functions
lessons.instruction: A cryptographic hash maps any message to a fixed-size digest. Hash "drillbox" with SHA-256 and print the digest length; a digest identifies content but does not conceal it.

lessons.title: Hash Collisions
lessons.instruction: A collision is two different inputs with the same digest. Use the deliberately weak sum-mod-10 hash to show that "ab" and "ba" collide; real systems need collision-resistant hashes.

lessons.title: Hashmaps
lessons.instruction: Go maps use hashes internally for comparable keys, but their iteration order is unspecified. Look up the digest name directly instead of depending on map order.

lessons.title: Deterministic
lessons.instruction: The same hash algorithm and bytes always produce the same digest. Hash identical messages twice and compare the fixed-size arrays directly.

lessons.title: One Way
lessons.instruction: Cryptographic hashes are designed to resist recovering an input from its digest. Verify a candidate by hashing it and comparing digests; there is no decrypt operation.

lessons.title: Toy Hash Function
lessons.instruction: Implement a tiny byte-sum hash to see compression and collisions firsthand. Return the sum modulo 256 for "abc"; never use this construction for security.

lessons.title: Toy Hash Review
lessons.instruction: A useful cryptographic hash changes drastically when one input bit changes. Confirm SHA-256 gives different digests for nearby messages; the earlier byte-sum toy does not provide this avalanche behavior.

lessons.title: What Is Message Integrity?
lessons.instruction: Integrity means detecting unauthorized changes; authenticity means knowing who produced the message. A plain hash can detect accidental changes only when its trusted expected digest arrives separately.

lessons.title: Message Authentication Code (MAC)
lessons.instruction: A MAC combines a secret key with a message so parties sharing the key can detect tampering and authenticate the sender as a key holder. Create an HMAC-SHA-256 tag.

lessons.title: Verify a MAC
lessons.instruction: Recompute a tag with the same key and compare it with hmac.Equal, which avoids timing-sensitive byte-by-byte comparisons. Verify the original message, not a modified one.

lessons.title: Hash-Based Message Authentication Code
lessons.instruction: HMAC safely combines a cryptographic hash with a key; simply prepending a secret to a message is not a replacement. Check that HMAC-SHA-256 reports a 32-byte tag size.

lessons.title: Toy HMAC
lessons.instruction: Use Go's HMAC construction rather than inventing one. Produce a tag for a message, then verify it with the same key and hmac.Equal.

lessons.title: MACs and JWTs
lessons.instruction: An HS256 JWT uses HMAC-SHA-256: every verifier needs the same secret and can therefore mint tokens too. JWT payloads are encoded, not encrypted.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	verifierCanSign := false
	payloadIsEncrypted := true
	fmt.Println(verifierCanSign, payloadIsEncrypted)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	verifierCanSign := true
	payloadIsEncrypted := false
	fmt.Println(verifierCanSign, payloadIsEncrypted)
}

lessons.title: Asymmetric JWTs
lessons.instruction: With an asymmetric JWT algorithm, the issuer signs with a private key while services verify with a public key. That separation lets verifiers validate tokens without gaining signing authority.

lessons.title: Asymmetric JWT Review
lessons.instruction: A signature covers the exact bytes that were signed. Sign a token-like payload with Ed25519 and confirm that changing the role makes verification fail.

lessons.title: Key Derivation Functions
lessons.instruction: A KDF derives fixed-size key material from an input secret plus parameters such as a salt and context. Password KDFs also add memory or CPU cost; a plain fast hash is not enough.

lessons.title: Argon2 – Storing Passwords
lessons.instruction: Store a password verifier, never the password. Argon2id PHC strings record the algorithm, version, cost parameters, salt, and derived hash so verification can reproduce the work.

lessons.title: Argon2 PHC Review
lessons.instruction: A PHC-formatted Argon2id verifier is self-describing. Split one into fields and identify its algorithm and parameter section; the salt and hash remain encoded data, not secrets.

lessons.title: Salts
lessons.instruction: Generate a fresh random salt for every password. Salts need not be secret; uniqueness prevents identical passwords from sharing verifiers and defeats reusable precomputed tables.

lessons.title: Why Are KDFs Slow?
lessons.instruction: Password KDFs deliberately make each guess costly, slowing offline attackers as well as legitimate verification. Tune cost on production hardware and increase it over time; do not add arbitrary sleeps.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fastHashSuitableForPasswords := true
	attackerPaysCostPerGuess := false
	fmt.Println(fastHashSuitableForPasswords, attackerPaysCostPerGuess)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fastHashSuitableForPasswords := false
	attackerPaysCostPerGuess := true
	fmt.Println(fastHashSuitableForPasswords, attackerPaysCostPerGuess)
}
